why: Take each statement in turn. The inductive effect is the permanent displacement of the shared electrons of a **sigma** bond towards the more electronegative atom, and it is relayed from one \(\sigma\) bond to the next along the chain — so statement (a), which puts it on a \(\pi\) bond, is false and statement (c) is true. The resonance (mesomeric) effect is the delocalisation of \(\pi\) electrons of a conjugated system, or of a lone pair on an atom attached to a \(\pi\) bond — it is transmitted through a chain of conjugated \(\pi\) bonds, so statement (b), which puts it on a \(\sigma\) bond, is false and statement (d) is true. The true pair is therefore (c) and (d). The remaining alternatives each carry at least one false statement. The pairing of the first two statements contains both of the false ones; the pairing of the first with the third fails because the first statement is false; and the pairing of the second with the third fails because the second statement is false.

why: Hyperconjugation is the delocalisation of the \(\sigma\) electrons of a C-H bond on an \(\alpha\)-carbon into an adjacent orbital that can accept them. In the ethyl carbocation the acceptor is the **empty p orbital** on the positively charged carbon, so the overlap is between a \(\sigma\) (C-H) orbital and a p orbital. \(\sigma - \sigma\) is wrong because one partner must be the p orbital (or the \(\pi\) system built from p orbitals) — overlap of two \(\sigma\) orbitals is not a delocalisation at all. \(p - p\) overlap is what forms an ordinary \(\pi\) bond, and \(\pi - \pi\) overlap is conjugation, that is resonance; neither involves the \(\sigma\) C-H bond that gives hyperconjugation its name. Note that where the acceptor is an alkene rather than a carbocation the same effect is described as \(\sigma - \pi\) conjugation, but no such alternative is offered here and the \(\sigma\)-with-p description is the one drawn in the chapter.

why: The compound intended is but-2-ene, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3}\). Each doubly bonded carbon carries two **different** groups (a \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) and an H), and rotation about a C=C double bond is not free, so the molecule exists as two separate, isolable forms — cis and trans. That is geometrical isomerism. The other three fail for a different reason each. Position and chain isomerism are relationships between the given compound and a **different** compound (but-1-ene, and 2-methylprop-1-ene, respectively); neither gives two forms of \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-CH_3}\) itself, which is what the question asks. Tautomerism needs a proton able to shift reversibly between two atoms, typically the \(\alpha\)-hydrogen of a carbonyl compound moving to oxygen; this hydrocarbon has no such second atom to receive a proton.

why: Read the zig-zag: the main chain runs through six vertices, and a one-carbon (methyl) stub hangs off the third of them, on the same carbon that carries the double bond. So the parent chain containing the C=C is six carbons long — hex-ene, not hept-ene — and it carries one methyl substituent. Numbering from the end that reaches the double bond first gives the double bond between C3 and C4 from either end, so the tie is broken by the substituent, which is at C3 from the left and C4 from the right; the lower locant set puts the methyl at C3. The name is 3-methylhex-3-ene. 'hept-3-ene' would require seven carbons in one unbranched chain, but the seventh carbon here is a branch, not part of the chain. 'hex-3-ene' has the right chain and the right double-bond position but omits the methyl group altogether. '2-ethylpent-2-ene' would need a two-carbon branch, and in any case names a five-carbon parent when a six-carbon chain through the double bond is available.

why: A carbocation carries only six valence electrons on the positive carbon — three bonding pairs and no lone pair. Three \(\sigma\) bonds and no lone pair means \(\mathrm{sp^2}\) hybridisation, so the three bonds lie in one plane at about \(120^\circ\) and the unhybridised \(\mathrm{p_z}\) orbital, which is empty, stands perpendicular to that plane. The shape is therefore trigonal planar. 'linear' would need \(\mathrm{sp}\) hybridisation, that is only two \(\sigma\) bonds; 'tetrahedral' would need four \(\sigma\) bonds and \(\mathrm{sp^3}\) hybridisation, which is the geometry of the neutral carbon it came from, not of the cation; 'octahedral' would need six bonds, which carbon can never form.

why: An alcohol is an alkane in which one hydrogen has been replaced by -OH, so its formula is (alkyl group) + OH. The alkyl group derived from \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+2}}\) by removing one H is \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+1}}\), giving \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+1}OH}\). Test it: \(n = 1\) gives \(\mathrm{CH_3OH}\) (methanol) and \(n = 2\) gives \(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\) (ethanol), both correct. The others fail the same test at \(n = 1\): \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n+2}OH}\) gives \(\mathrm{CH_4OH}\), which is a carbon with five bonds; \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n-2}OH}\) gives \(\mathrm{CH_0OH}\), which has no hydrogen on carbon at all; and \(\mathrm{C_nH_{2n}OH}\) gives \(\mathrm{CH_2OH}\), a free radical rather than a stable molecule.

why: The description names two things at once — the electrons being delocalised come from a **sigma** bond, and the orbital they spread into is a **p** orbital. That combination is exactly hyperconjugation, which the chapter defines as delocalisation of the \(\sigma\) electrons of an \(\alpha\) C-H bond into an empty p orbital, a p orbital holding an unpaired electron, or an adjacent unsaturated system. The inductive effect involves no orbital overlap of this kind — it is a displacement of a \(\sigma\) bonding pair towards a more electronegative atom, with the electrons staying in that bond. Resonance is the delocalisation of \(\pi\) electrons or of a lone pair through a conjugated system, so its donor is not a \(\sigma\) bond. 'Electronic effect' is the umbrella term covering inductive, resonance, electromeric and hyperconjugative effects together, so it does not name this particular one.
